name: Casio MT-40
originalPurpose: A cheap home keyboard with built-in preset rhythms and instrument sounds, sold to hobbyists rather than professional musicians.
whatActuallyHappened: Its built-in 'rock' rhythm preset, designed by Casio engineer Hiroko Okuda, became the entire backing track of Wayne Smith's 'Under Mi Sleng Teng' (1985), produced by Prince Jammy, after musician Noel Davey reached for it because he could not afford the Yamaha DX7 he wanted. The riddim it created has since been re-recorded by more Jamaican artists than any other in reggae history and began the genre's fully computerized era.
priceStory: A budget home keyboard, around 150 US dollars new, next to a professional synthesizer costing several times that; the record it created came directly out of that price gap.
hook: A cheap home keyboard's demo button ended dub's analogue era.
blurb: The Casio MT-40 was a budget home keyboard with built-in rhythm patterns, sold to people who could never afford a real studio synthesizer. A Casio engineer designed its 'rock' preset for that market, with no thought of reggae. In 1985, musician Noel Davey could not afford the synthesizer he originally wanted, which cost many times more, so he used the MT-40's rock preset to build the backing track for Wayne Smith's 'Under Mi Sleng Teng', produced by Prince Jammy. The price is the direct reason the record exists at all. It became one of the most re-recorded rhythms in reggae history and began the genre's digital era, the clearest case on this map of a hobbyist's home product crossing into a genre it was never built for.
